intro: A eulogy doesn't have to cover a whole life. A few true, personal memories usually say more than a long list of facts.

list: Jot down stories, sayings, habits and moments, and ask family and friends for theirs.
Don't worry about order yet.
What sums them up? Their kindness, their humour, a love of the garden. Choose a story for each.
Who they were to you, two or three stories, and a short goodbye. Around three to five minutes is common; check with the celebrant.
Use your own words and short sentences. Read it aloud and change anything that feels awkward.

p: Print it in large type with gaps where you'll pause. It's completely fine to ask someone else to read it, or to stand beside you. Be gentle with yourself; if grief feels too much, bereavement support services can help.

title: How much fabric do I need for a quilt? Backing, binding and borders
description: Measure the finished size, add for backing overhang, work out binding from the perimeter, and buy a little extra for shrinkage and mistakes.
intro: Most fabric mistakes happen on the backing and binding, especially when you resize a pattern. A few simple calculations prevent them.

list: Decide the finished quilt width and length. Common sizes: baby, lap or throw, twin, queen and king; check a size chart if you're unsure.
Add about 4 inches (10 cm) to each side for quilting overhang.
If the quilt is wider than your fabric, you'll need to join widths, or use extra-wide backing fabric.
Measure the perimeter (2 × width + 2 × length), add about 10 to 15 inches for corners and joining, and divide by your usable fabric width to find how many strips to cut.
Add up the length of every border and sashing strip, including corners, before you buy.

p: Fabric can shrink when washed, and cutting mistakes happen. Many quilters add around 10% or a quarter-yard to each fabric. Write the numbers down before you go to the shop.

title: How to remember to pray for people after you've promised
description: Write it down the moment you promise, keep one simple list, pray through a few names each day, and follow up with the person.
intro: 'I'll pray for you' is easy to say and easy to forget. A small routine helps you keep the promise.

list: Write the name and request down the moment you say you'll pray: a note on your phone or a small notebook.
Keep all requests in one place, so nothing gets lost in texts and scraps of paper.
If the list is long, split it across the days of the week, so each person is remembered regularly.
Mark when a situation changes or a request is answered. Looking back can be encouraging.

p: A short message to say you've been thinking of them, and to ask how things are, means a lot.

title: Why can't I wheelie? The usual reasons and a drill for each
description: Check your gear and seat height, lean back with straight arms instead of pulling, cover the rear brake, and work up in small steps.
intro: Most riders who can't wheelie make the same few mistakes. Fix them one at a time, on grass, with a helmet on.

list: Try an easy-to-middle gear: too easy and you spin out, too hard and you can't lift.
A slightly lower seat can make it easier to lean back.
Straight arms, and shift your weight back as you push a pedal stroke. Pulling hard with bent arms brings the wheel up then straight back down.
Keep a finger on the rear brake at all times. A light tap brings the front down and stops you looping out. It's what makes it safe to go higher.
Practise lifting higher and catching it with the brake, without pedalling. You're looking for the point where it feels light.

p: Once you can hold the lift, add one pedal stroke at a time. Short, regular sessions beat long frustrating ones. Practise on grass or a quiet flat area away from traffic.

title: How to bond two rabbits that keep fighting
description: Neuter both, start side by side, swap scents, meet in a neutral space, keep sessions short, and separate at the first real fight.
intro: Bonding can take days or months. Going slowly and stopping before fights escalate usually works better than pushing on.

list: Both rabbits should be neutered and fully healed, usually several weeks after surgery.
Have a vet check if either has injuries or health problems.
Keep them in pens next to each other so they can see and smell each other without contact.
Swap litter trays, toys or bedding between them every day or two.
Use a space neither rabbit thinks of as theirs. Keep the first sessions short, and end on a calm note.

p: Mounting and chasing can be normal. A tight ball of fighting is not: separate them straight away, with a towel or thick gloves to protect your hands, and go back a step. See an exotics vet after any injury. Many rescues and rabbit charities offer bonding help.

title: How to get a campsite at a park that's always sold out
description: Know when sites are released, be ready at that moment, watch for cancellations, try weekdays and shoulder seasons, and keep a backup campground.
intro: Popular campgrounds often fill within minutes of release. A bit of planning improves your chances a lot.

list: Many US federal campgrounds release sites on a rolling basis, often about six months ahead. Check the campground's own page for its exact rule and time zone.

sections.h: Be ready at the moment of release
list: Log in early, have your dates, site choices and payment ready, and know your second and third choices.
Lots of people cancel in the last week or two before their trip. Check often, or use a cancellation alert.
Weekdays and the shoulder seasons (spring and autumn) are much easier than summer weekends. Shorter stays can also fit gaps.

p: Nearby national forest, state park or first-come, first-served campgrounds can save the trip. Always book through the official site, and check the rules before you go.

title: How much to set aside for taxes from side-gig income (US)
description: Set aside a share of every payout in a separate account, track expenses and mileage, and know the quarterly estimated-tax dates.
intro: Gig and freelance income usually has no tax taken out, so the bill can be a shock. This is general information, not tax advice.

list: Move a share of each payout into a separate savings account as soon as it arrives. Many people start somewhere around 25 to 30%, then adjust once they know their real tax picture.
On top of income tax, self-employed people generally pay self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare). That's often what catches people out.
Keep records of business expenses and business miles. They can reduce the income you're taxed on.

The IRS generally expects estimated payments if you'll owe $1,000 or more for the year. Payments are usually due around 15 April, 15 June, 15 September and 15 January (dates shift for weekends and holidays).

p: Check IRS guidance on estimated taxes, or ask a tax professional, especially in your first year of side income.

title: What to build from a big mixed bin of bricks
description: Sort lightly by type, pick builds that use common pieces, rebuild an old set, or set a simple challenge.
intro: A big mixed tub can feel useless because you can never find the right piece. A little light sorting and a few simple ideas make it fun again.

list: Split into a few trays: plates, bricks, slopes, wheels, people and odd bits. Twenty minutes is enough to start.

sections.h: Pick builds that use common pieces
list: Houses, vehicles, towers, animals and robots can all be made from basic bricks and plates.
If you still have the instructions (or can find them online), rebuilding an old set is a good way to find out what's there.
'Build something that rolls', 'build the tallest tower with 50 pieces', or 'build your bedroom'. Limits spark ideas.

p: Small pieces are a choking hazard for young children; follow the age guidance on the original boxes.

title: How to solve hard sudoku without guessing
description: Use pencil marks for every cell, then look for pairs, pointing pairs and X-wings before you ever guess.
intro: Hard puzzles usually need one or two techniques beyond the basics. Once you know what to look for, guessing is rarely needed.

list: Write every possible number in each empty cell. Many techniques only show up once all candidates are written.

sections.h: Look for naked and hidden pairs
list: Two cells in a row, column or box that can only be the same two numbers: remove those numbers from the rest of that unit.
If a number in a box can only go in one row or column, remove it from that row or column outside the box.
If a number can only go in the same two columns in two different rows, it can be removed from those columns elsewhere.

p: If you hit a contradiction, check recent entries first and confirm each against its row, column and box. Working in pencil makes mistakes easier to undo.

title: How to beatmatch by ear: hear which track is rushing
description: Start on the first beat, listen to the kick drums, decide which track is ahead, nudge it, then adjust the tempo, one small step at a time.
intro: Beatmatching by ear is a listening skill. Short, regular practice with two simple tracks gets most people there.

list: Use two tracks with clear, steady kick drums and similar tempos. Avoid busy intros at first.
Cue the incoming track on the first beat of a bar, often where the music starts or a big change happens. Count 1-2-3-4 along with it.
Release the incoming track on the '1' of the playing track. Listen in your headphones with one ear on the room.
If the kicks start to 'gallop' (two hits close together), they've drifted. Nudge the incoming track back or forward to line them up, then decide whether it's faster or slower.
Move the tempo slider a tiny amount in that direction, and check again.

p: Ten minutes a day beats a long weekend session. Once the kicks stay locked, practise phrasing: starting the new track at the start of a musical phrase, often 16 or 32 beats.

title: How to prove your broadband keeps dropping out
description: Log every drop with times, test with a cable, check the router, keep a call diary, and escalate in writing.
intro: Intermittent drops are hard to prove because the line often looks fine when the provider tests it. A clear record makes your case much stronger.

list: Note the date, the time it went off, the time it came back, and what you were doing. A connection monitor running on a spare device can do this automatically.
If you can, connect a computer to the router with a cable. If the cable connection drops too, the problem is more likely the line or the provider.
Note the router's lights when it drops. Many routers also keep a log of disconnections in their settings page.
For each call or chat: date, agent name, reference number, what they tested and what they promised.

p: If it isn't fixed, make a formal complaint in writing with your log attached. If it stays unresolved, check your regulator's guidance on complaints and dispute schemes (in the UK, Ofcom).

title: Planning your first model railway track plan for the space you have
description: Measure the space, decide what you enjoy, respect minimum curve radius and reach, start simple, and test with the track you own.
intro: Most first layouts go wrong on curves that are too tight and benchwork that's too deep to reach. Planning for those first saves a lot of rework.

list: Room size, doors, windows, sockets and anything you need to walk around. Draw it to scale on paper first.
Watching trains run (a loop) or shunting and operating (switching). It shapes the whole plan.

sections.h: Mind the curves and the reach
list: Check the minimum curve radius your locomotives and stock can handle in your scale; wider is smoother.
Keep any area you'll need to reach within about an arm's length, roughly 60 to 75 cm (2 to 2.5 ft), or add access.
Keep slopes gentle; steep grades limit how many wagons a locomotive can pull.

p: Lay the track you already own on the floor or board before fixing anything. Run trains, see what works, then build. A small finished layout beats a big unfinished one.

title: Stuck on an origami step? How to read the diagram
description: Learn the basic symbols, look ahead to the next picture, check your paper is the right way up, and practise the base folds.
intro: Most origami frustration comes from a handful of symbols and a few tricky moves. Once you know them, diagrams make much more sense.

list: Dashed line: valley fold (fold towards you). Dash-dot line: mountain fold (fold away).
Arrows show the direction of the fold; a looped arrow often means turn the paper over.
The next diagram shows what the result should look like. Working backwards from it often makes the step clear.
Many mistakes come from the paper being turned or flipped. Match your paper to the diagram before folding.
Square base, waterbomb base, bird base and fish base appear in hundreds of models. Learning them first makes harder models easier.

p: Make firm creases, and pre-crease difficult folds before collapsing them. If you're stuck, try the same step on a bigger sheet of paper.

title: Inherited a stamp collection? Where to start
description: Don't remove stamps from albums, sort by country and era, look for the few that stand out, and get anything promising looked at by an expert.
intro: Most inherited collections are mostly common stamps, with a few that deserve a closer look. A calm, careful sort helps you find them.

list: Don't peel stamps off album pages or covers, and don't clean them. Handle them by the edges, ideally with stamp tongs.
Group albums and loose stamps by country, then by rough era (Victorian, early 1900s, modern).
Older stamps in good condition, full sheets, unused stamps with gum, covers (envelopes) with interesting postmarks, and anything with certificates.
List what's in each album, with photos. It helps family decide, and helps any expert you ask.

p: A local stamp society, a reputable dealer or an auction house can tell you what's worth more attention. Catalogue prices are often much higher than what stamps sell for, so get a realistic opinion before selling.

title: How to identify a rock you found
description: Note where you found it, look at colour, grain and lustre, try simple streak, scratch and magnet tests, and compare with local guides.
intro: You can narrow down most finds with a few safe, simple checks. Where you found it is often the biggest clue.

list: Beach, river, quarry or field, and the area. Local geology narrows things down a lot.
Colour, whether it's grainy or smooth, any layers or crystals, and whether it's shiny (metallic) or dull. A cheap hand lens helps.
Streak: rub it on the back of an unglazed tile and note the colour of the powder.
Scratch: does a steel nail scratch it? Does it scratch glass?
Magnet: does a magnet stick to it?
Use a local field guide or a museum's online collection, or ask a local rock club. Photograph it in daylight next to a coin for scale.

p: Check the rules before keeping finds, especially in parks, on protected beaches and on public land. Never use acid tests without proper safety gear.

title: How to learn Excel fast before a new job starts
description: Find out what the job actually uses, learn the handful of everyday skills first, practise on realistic sheets for 15 to 20 minutes a day, and keep a cheat sheet.
intro: You don't need to know all of Excel. Most jobs use the same small set of skills, and a few days of focused practice covers a lot of it.

sections.h: Find out what the job uses
list: Ask your manager or recruiter what you'll do in spreadsheets: entering data, reports, rotas, budgets? It's a normal question to ask.
Moving around and selecting cells, simple formulas (SUM, AVERAGE), sorting and filtering, and formatting a table so it's readable.
Next: relative versus fixed references ($A$1), IF, a lookup (XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP), a simple pivot table and a chart.
Make or download a small sales list, a rota or a household budget, and do real tasks on it. Fifteen to twenty minutes a day beats one long cram.
Write down the steps and shortcuts you use most (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Arrow, F2 to edit a cell) and keep it next to you for your first weeks.

p: Break the task into small steps, try it on a copy so nothing can go wrong, and search for the exact thing you want to do. Experienced users look things up all the time too.

title: How to find where clothes moths and carpet beetles are breeding
description: Work out which pest you have, check the dark, undisturbed spots where larvae feed, deal with infested items, and use traps to see if numbers fall.
intro: The damage comes from larvae, not the flying adults, and they feed in quiet, dark places with natural fibres, dust or pet hair. Finding those spots matters more than spraying.

sections.h: Work out which pest you have
list: Clothes moth larvae leave silky tubes or webbing and irregular holes. Carpet beetle larvae are small, hairy and striped, and leave shed skins behind.
Photograph what you find next to a coin for scale.
Carpet edges and under heavy furniture, the backs of wardrobes and drawers, stored wool, cashmere, silk and feathers, rugs, upholstery, vents and anywhere pet hair or lint collects.
Wash on the hottest setting the fabric allows, dry clean, or bag and freeze items for about a week. Then store clean items in sealed bags or boxes.
Vacuum edges, crevices and under furniture thoroughly, and empty the vacuum outside. Repeat regularly for several weeks, since eggs keep hatching.

p: Pheromone traps catch adult male clothes moths and show whether numbers are falling. Note the date and count each time you check. If the numbers don't drop after a few months, or the damage is widespread, call a licensed pest-control professional. Follow product labels for any chemical treatment, especially around pets, birds and children.

title: How to order wine at a restaurant when you know nothing about wine
description: Decide your budget, say what you usually like in plain words, use a few wine-list terms, and ask the staff. It's what they're there for.
intro: You don't need to know grape names or regions. A budget, a rough idea of what you like, and a couple of plain questions get you a good bottle or glass.

list: Pick a price range on the list before you read anything else. Many people choose the second-cheapest wine; anything in your range is fine.
Dry: not sweet. Most red and many white wines are dry.
Light- or full-bodied: how heavy and rich it feels in your mouth, like skimmed milk versus cream.
Oaked: aged in oak, often tasting of vanilla or toast. Unoaked tastes fresher.
Tannic: the drying feeling some reds leave, like strong tea.
Use plain words: 'something light and fresh', 'a fruity red that isn't too heavy', 'not sweet'. Mention a wine you liked if you remember it.

p: Point to a price on the list and say 'something like this'. It tells them your budget without saying it out loud. Then ask what they'd suggest with your food.
Take a photo of the label of anything you enjoy, with a word or two about why. Next time you'll know where to start. Always drink responsibly and only if you're of legal drinking age.

title: How to find a perfume that suits you without wasting money
description: Work out which notes you like, test on skin rather than paper, wait a few hours before deciding, and sample before buying a full bottle.
intro: Perfume changes on your skin over a few hours, so the first sniff of a tester rarely tells you enough. A bit of method saves a lot of money.

sections.h: Start from what you already like
list: Think of scents you've enjoyed: a friend's perfume, a candle, a shower gel. Note words like woody, vanilla, citrus, floral, fresh or spicy, and what you dislike.
Paper strips are fine for narrowing down, but try your top one or two on your wrist or inner elbow. Don't rub, and test no more than two or three a day.
Smell it again after an hour and after four hours. The scent you'll live with is the later stage, not the first spray.
Ask for a sample, buy a small decant or travel spray, and wear it for a few days in different situations before committing to a full bottle.

p: Write down the name, the notes, and how it smelled at each stage. Patterns soon appear, and they help you find similar scents and cheaper alternatives. Stop using anything that irritates your skin.

title: How to learn tarot card meanings without the guidebook
description: Learn the structure first (Major Arcana and four suits), study one suit at a time, read the pictures, practise three-card spreads, and keep a journal.
intro: 78 cards sounds like a lot, but the deck has a clear structure. Learn the pattern and most meanings follow from it.

list: 22 Major Arcana cards for big themes, and 56 Minor Arcana in four suits: Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles, each running Ace to Ten plus four court cards.
Learn each suit's theme first (Cups for feelings and relationships, Pentacles for work and material things, and so on), then how the numbers build from Ace to Ten.
In Rider-Waite-style decks the imagery tells the story. Describe what's happening in the card in your own words before checking the book.
Draw three cards and write a few lines on how they connect. Then compare with the traditional meanings.

p: Note each card you draw and what it meant to you. Reviewing your notes is what makes meanings stick. Treat tarot as reflection and symbolism, not as a basis for health, money or legal decisions.

title: How to practise sleight of hand so it doesn't look obvious
description: Practise slowly, film yourself from the audience's angle, watch for the common giveaways, and only perform a move once it passes on camera.
intro: Most moves look obvious not because the method is wrong but because of small tells: tension, pauses, angles and where you look. Filming yourself shows them.

list: Learn the move slowly and smoothly before trying to speed up. Speed hides nothing if the move is jerky.
Prop your phone where a spectator's eyes would be, at a table and standing. A mirror helps, but a recording shows what you actually do.
Flashing: the audience glimpses a hidden card.
Tension: stiff fingers or a cramped grip.
Pauses: a hitch right at the moment of the move.
Eye line: looking at your hands when you should look at the audience.
Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour once a week. Do a few slow reps, then a few at performance speed, and film the last one.

p: When a move looks clean on camera from every angle you'll be seen from, try it on a friend. Keep notes of what they noticed and go back to the camera.

title: Pool chemistry for beginners: what to test and what to add
description: Know your pool's volume, test regularly, fix one thing at a time (usually alkalinity, then pH, then sanitiser), follow the label and retest before adding more.
intro: Pool water comes down to a few numbers. Test them, change one at a time, and give each change time to work.

list: Every dose depends on how many litres or gallons your pool or tub holds. Work it out once (length x width x average depth for a rectangle) and write it down.
Test at least weekly, more in hot weather or heavy use. Strips are quick; drop kits are usually more accurate. Test before adding anything.
Sanitiser (free chlorine or bromine): kills germs and algae.
pH: how acidic the water is. It affects comfort and how well chlorine works.
Total alkalinity: helps keep pH steady.
Cyanuric acid (outdoor chlorine pools): protects chlorine from sunlight.

sections.h: Fix one thing at a time
list: A common order is alkalinity first, then pH, then sanitiser. Circulate, wait for the time on the label, and retest before adding more.

p: Always read and follow the product label. Never mix pool chemicals with each other, add chemicals to water and never water to chemicals, store them apart in a cool, dry place away from children, and keep everyone out of the water until levels are back in range. For green water you can't clear, equipment problems or leaks, call a pool professional.

title: What the symbols on clothing care labels mean
description: Five basic shapes cover almost every label: a tub for washing, a triangle for bleach, a square for drying, an iron for ironing and a circle for professional cleaning.
intro: Care labels use the same five shapes almost everywhere. Dots usually mean heat (more dots, hotter), lines under a symbol mean gentler, and a cross means don't.

list: A tub with a number or dots shows the maximum temperature: one dot is about 30°C (86°F), two about 40°C (104°F), three about 50°C (122°F), four about 60°C (140°F).
One line under the tub means a gentler (synthetic or permanent press) cycle; two lines mean a very gentle or wool cycle.
A hand in the tub means hand wash only. A crossed-out tub means don't wash in water.
An empty triangle means any bleach is OK. A triangle with two diagonal lines means non-chlorine bleach only. A crossed-out triangle means no bleach.
A circle in a square means tumble dry; dots show the heat (one low, two normal). A crossed-out one means don't tumble dry.
A square with a curved line at the top means line dry, one horizontal line means dry flat, and three vertical lines mean drip dry.
One dot means a cool iron (about 110°C), two dots medium (about 150°C), three dots hot (about 200°C). A crossed-out iron means don't iron.

p: A circle means dry cleaning or professional wet cleaning; the letter inside tells the cleaner which process to use. A crossed-out circle means don't dry clean. When you're unsure, wash cooler and gentler, and air dry. For stain removers and bleach, follow the product label and never mix cleaning products.

title: How not to get lost hiking: five habits for people with no sense of direction
description: Plan the route's key turns, use handrails like rivers and ridges, check in with the map often, look back regularly, and know what to do if you think you've gone wrong.
intro: Getting lost usually starts with a few minutes of not checking. A handful of simple habits keeps you on track, even if you have a poor sense of direction.

sections.h: Brief the route before you go
list: Look at the map at home. Note the key turns, the 'handrails' you'll follow (paths, rivers, walls, ridges) and a 'too far' marker that tells you you've overshot.
At every junction and every 15 to 20 minutes, find yourself on the map and name the last thing you passed. Small checks are easier than big corrections.
Set the map so north on the map points north on the ground (use a compass or your phone). Then what's ahead of you on the map is ahead of you for real.
Turn around now and then, especially at junctions. The way back looks different, and you'll recognise it if you need to retrace your steps.

sections.h: If you think you've gone wrong
p: Stop. Don't keep walking in hope. Go back to the last place you were sure of, or use the map, compass or GPS to work out where you are. Always carry a proper map, check the weather, tell someone your route and when you'll be back, and call the emergency services if you're in danger.
